bibl.title: Inhibitory Actions Unified by Network Integration

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether divisive and subtractive suppression can be assigned to particular interneuron types at all
span.quote: One common, conceptually straightforward framework models the effects of synaptic inhibition as a linear transformation with a divisive (scaling) and a subtractive (shifting) component ( Chance and Abbott, 2000 ; Doiron et al., 2001 ; Mitchell and Silver, 2003 ; Prescott and De Koninck, 2003 ; Hao et al., 2009 ). In this view, the essential question is whether the suppression that an interneuron type provides is predominantly divisive or predominantly subtractive

span.label: how activating somatostatin- or parvalbumin-positive interneurons changes auditory cortical responses to tones
span.quote: We evaluated how optogenetically activating somatostatin- and parvalbumin-positive interneurons subtractively or divisively suppressed auditory cortical cells’ responses to tones. In both awake and anesthetized animals, we found that activating either family of interneurons produced mixtures of divisive and subtractive effects and that simultaneously recorded neurons were often suppressed in qualitatively different ways.

span.label: the suppression type specific to an interneuron class can be masked by the network it is embedded in, so the property is not a property of the class
span.quote: We conclude that the characteristics of response inhibition specific to a single interneuron type can be “masked” by the network configuration and cellular properties of the network in which they are embedded.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: A simple network model shows that threshold nonlinearities can interact with network activity to transform subtractive inhibition of neurons into divisive inhibition of networks, or vice versa.

span.label: divisive versus subtractive cortical inhibition
span.quote: We evaluated how optogenetically activating somatostatin- and parvalbumin-positive interneurons subtractively or divisively suppressed auditory cortical cells’ responses to tones.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: We then used linear 16-channel silicon probes to record the responses of isolated single units across the auditory cortical layers to pure-tone acoustic stimulation with and without blue-light illumination of the cortical surface.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Threshold nonlinearity in a convergent network converts the linear suppression type: suppressed inputs falling below the output neuron's spiking threshold turn subtractive inhibition of single neurons into divisive inhibition of the network, and vice versa
span.quote: As one example of such a mechanism, we used a simple network model to show that threshold nonlinearities can interact with inhibition to transform subtractive inhibition of neurons into divisive inhibition of networks, or vice versa.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Because most cortical input to a neuron is intracortical, activating interneurons changes the firing of the neuron's own converging and recurrent inputs, adding a second-order effect on top of the direct linear effect on that neuron
span.quote: Thus, although changes in inhibitory tone may have the predicted linear effect on neurons’ responses to any particular current or conductance, they also change the firing properties of the majority of these neurons’ converging/recurrent inputs and may thus have effects on responses qualitatively different from those predicted by single-neuron models.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Rectification of input firing rates (rates cannot go negative) makes subtractive suppression act most strongly at each input neuron's preferred frequency, which the connectivity function then passes on as a divisive-looking loss of drive at the target's best frequency
span.quote: Because firing rates cannot be negative, subtractive suppression hasagreater effectatthe center of each input neuron’s tuning profile

span.label: most cortical input is intracortical, so changing inhibition changes the firing of a neuron's own inputs as well as the neuron, producing effects single-neuron models do not predict
span.quote: To explain this observation, we note that cortical neurons are densely interconnected: the majority of cortical neurons receive the majority of their inputs from intracortical or feedback connections rather than from feedforward thalamocortical projections ( Benshalom and White, 1986 ; Abeles, 1991 ). Thus, although changes in inhibitory tone may have the predicted linear effect on neurons’ responses to any particular current or conductance, they also change the firing properties of the majority of these neurons’ converging/recurrent inputs and may thus have effects on responses qualitatively different from those predicted by single-neuron models.

span.label: in a network model, threshold nonlinearities plus the strength of suppression of a cell's inputs determine whether the observed effect looks divisive, subtractive or both
span.quote: As one example of such a mechanism, we used a simple network model to show that threshold nonlinearities can interact with inhibition to transform subtractive inhibition of neurons into divisive inhibition of networks, or vice versa. Varying just two properties of the model neuron (its threshold and the overall strength of suppression of its inputs) could cause the apparent linear effect of inhibition to be divisive, subtractive, or both

span.label: the character of suppression in downstream neurons is set by their own thresholds and connections rather than by what happened upstream
span.quote: The character of suppression in higher-order neurons was determined by their intrinsic properties and connections, regardless of whether the suppression in first-order neurons was divisive or subtractive— in other words, the characteristics of response inhibition specific to a single interneuron type can be “masked” by the network configuration and cellular properties of the network in which they are embedded.

span.label: further sources of the same masking are available: interneurons are themselves tuned and receive organised excitation, and many types inhibit one another
span.quote: Note that this second-order effect of inhibitory activity on excitatory tuning is merely one among many mechanisms by which this “masking” phenomenon may emerge. Additional sources of obfuscation are abundant in the cortical literature. For example, many types of interneuron are themselves tuned and receive organized excitation from local cortical networks ( Thomson et al., 2002 ; Holmgren et al., 2003 ; Yoshimura and Callaway, 2005 ; Stokes and Isaacson, 2010 ; Moore and Wehr, 2013 ; Lee et al., 2014 ); manipulations that change the tuning of cortical excitation will themselves change the tuning of cortical interneurons, producing third- and higher-order effects. In addition, many types of cortical interneurons selectively inhibit one another; activation of one type may thus reduce the inhibition originating from others, producing complex changes in activity and tuning ( Jiang et al., 2013 ; Lee et al., 2013 ; Pi et al., 2013 ; Xu et al., 2013 ; Fu et al., 2014 ). It is thus likely that similar masking phenomena will be observed in any network of appreciable complexity.

span.label: local subnetworks with different intrinsic or connectional properties can interpret the same inhibition differently
span.quote: This indicates that even in the same global network, local subnetworks of neurons with different intrinsic or connectional properties can selectively and differentially interpret the inhibition provided by a given population of interneurons.

span.label: Both interneuron populations were driven nonselectively and with diffuse timing, unlike their natural recruitment, so type-specific functional differences may have been washed out.
span.quote: However, we note that in this experiment both populations of interneurons were activated in a nonselective and temporally diffuse manner; it is likely that during normal brain operation, functional differences between interneuron types will emerge from differences in their response properties and temporal dynamics.

span.label: Optogenetic stimulation parameters were not matched between the awake and anesthetized preparations.
span.quote: The similarity of the data in the anesthetized and the awake preparation, despite the fact that some of the optogenetic parameters (light strength, optical fiber diameter) were not identical between the two conditions, suggests that this masking may be relatively robust.

span.label: The proposed network mechanism is only one of several possible routes to the masking effect, and the paper does not exclude the others it lists.
span.quote: Note that this second-order effect of inhibitory activity on excitatory tuning is merely one among many mechanisms by which this “masking” phenomenon may emerge.

span.label: both interneuron populations were driven nonselectively and diffusely in time, so differences arising from their natural response dynamics would not appear here
span.quote: However, we note that in this experiment both populations of interneurons were activated in a nonselective and temporally diffuse manner; it is likely that during normal brain operation, functional differences between interneuron types will emerge from differences in their response properties and temporal dynamics.

span.label: the masking mechanism demonstrated is offered as one among many rather than as the mechanism
span.quote: Note that this second-order effect of inhibitory activity on excitatory tuning is merely one among many mechanisms by which this “masking” phenomenon may emerge. Additional sources of obfuscation are abundant in the cortical literature. For example, many types of interneuron are themselves tuned and receive organized excitation from local cortical networks ( Thomson et al., 2002 ; Holmgren et al., 2003 ; Yoshimura and Callaway, 2005 ; Stokes and Isaacson, 2010 ; Moore and Wehr, 2013 ; Lee et al., 2014 ); manipulations that change the tuning of cortical excitation will themselves change the tuning of cortical interneurons, producing third- and higher-order effects. In addition, many types of cortical interneurons selectively inhibit one another; activation of one type may thus reduce the inhibition originating from others, producing complex changes in activity and tuning ( Jiang et al., 2013 ; Lee et al., 2013 ; Pi et al., 2013 ; Xu et al., 2013 ; Fu et al., 2014 ). It is thus likely that similar masking phenomena will be observed in any network of appreciable complexity.

span.label: the driver lines are stated to have under ten percent misexpression, which bounds but does not remove off-target activation
span.quote: In Ai32 × Sst-Cre mice (“Ai32/ Sst”), GFP and Pvalb did not colocalize ( Figure 1A ), while in Ai32 × Pvalb-Cre mice (“Ai32/Pvalb”), GFP and Pvalb did co-localize ( Figure 1H ). This is consistent with expression patterns established by numerous groups ( Cardin et al., 2009 ; Sohal et al., 2009 ; Cardin et al., 2010 ; Kerlin et al., 2010 ; Taniguchi et al., 2011 ; Adesnik et al., 2012 ; Kvitsiani et al., 2013 ; Pfeffer et al., 2013 ) who found low (<10%) levels of misexpression within the cortex.

span.label: the divisive/subtractive decomposition, carried from cable theory into claims about interneuron classes in intact cortex
span.quote: One common, conceptually straightforward framework models the effects of synaptic inhibition as a linear transformation with a divisive (scaling) and a subtractive (shifting) component ( Chance and Abbott, 2000 ; Doiron et al., 2001 ; Mitchell and Silver, 2003 ; Prescott and De Koninck, 2003 ; Hao et al., 2009 ). In this view, the essential question is whether the suppression that an interneuron type provides is predominantly divisive or predominantly subtractive

span.label: a minimal threshold-nonlinear network used to show that the transformation between the two is possible in principle
span.quote: A simple network model shows that threshold nonlinearities can interact with network activity to transform subtractive inhibition of neurons into divisive inhibition of networks, or vice versa. Varying threshold and the strength of suppression of a model neuron could determine whether the effect of inhibition appeared divisive, subtractive, or both.

span.label: DIVISIVE and SUBTRACTIVE are defined here as parameters of a straight line fitted to suppressed against control responses - slope below one is divisive, intercept below zero is subtractive - so they are properties of a FIT, not observed categories
span.quote: In a subtractively suppressed neuron, this best-fit line will have a slope of 1 and a y-intercept significantly less than 0, while in a divisively suppressed neuron, the best-fit line will have a slope significantly less than 1 and a y-intercept not significantly different from 0.

span.label: the framework's central question presupposes that the answer belongs to the interneuron type; this paper's result is that the question is asked at the wrong level
span.quote: One common, conceptually straightforward framework models the effects of synaptic inhibition as a linear transformation with a divisive (scaling) and a subtractive (shifting) component ( Chance and Abbott, 2000 ; Doiron et al., 2001 ; Mitchell and Silver, 2003 ; Prescott and De Koninck, 2003 ; Hao et al., 2009 ). In this view, the essential question is whether the suppression that an interneuron type provides is predominantly divisive or predominantly subtractive

span.label: the anatomical prediction is precise and well founded - dendritic synapses change current without changing somatic conductance, perisomatic ones change conductance - and it is confirmed in vitro on single cells
span.quote: Under many conditions, somatic and dendritic inhibition have been confirmed to provide divisive and subtractive suppression, respectively, to single pyramidal neurons in vitro

span.label: the decisive observation is that neurons recorded AT THE SAME TIME on the same probe are suppressed in different ways, which rules out animal-to-animal and preparation variability by construction
span.quote: This variability is unlikely to be an artifact of animal-to-animal variability in the experimental preparation, because the characteristics of suppression in simultaneously recorded cells were not strongly correlated ( Figure 4 ), and it is unlikely to be associated only with a specific anesthetic condition because we observed it in awake animals as well.

span.label: light was set to a level that suppressed firing to about half of control in most units, so the manipulation is calibrated by its effect rather than by its intensity
span.quote: Recordings were performed with a light power near 40 µW (range 25 to 100 µW), which typically suppressed firing to about 50% of control in 65%–75% of units

span.label: replicates → prior reports of low (<10%) misexpression in Sst-Cre and Pvalb-Cre driver lines (Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009; Cardin et al., 2010; Kerlin et al., 2010; Taniguchi et al., 2011; Adesnik et al., 2012; Kvitsiani et al., 2013; Pfeffer et al., 2013)
span.quote: This is consistent with expression patterns established by numerous groups ( Cardin et al., 2009 ; Sohal et al., 2009 ; Cardin et al., 2010 ; Kerlin et al., 2010 ; Taniguchi et al., 2011 ; Adesnik et al., 2012 ; Kvitsiani et al., 2013 ; Pfeffer et al., 2013 ) who found low (<10%) levels of misexpression within the cortex.

span.label: critiques → the framework in which each interneuron type is assigned a fixed divisive or subtractive function
span.quote: This framework has been applied to visual cortex by several groups with seemingly conflicting results ( Atallah et al., 2012 , 2014 ; Lee et al., 2012 , 2014 ; Wilson et al., 2012 ; El-Boustani and Sur, 2014 ; Xue et al., 2014 ), producing an ongoing debate regarding whether separate functions of division and subtraction can be assigned to different populations of interneuron and whether those assignments are fixed.

span.label: reconciles → the apparently irreconcilable visual cortex findings about Sst and Pvalb interneuron effects
span.quote: Studies in primary visual cortex (V1) have produced diverse and even apparently irreconcilable findings regarding the effects of activating Sst+ and Pvalb+ interneurons on single unit responses. Various studies have shown that Pvalb+ neurons’ activation may change other neurons’ sensory responses divisively, while Sst+ neurons’ activation produces subtractive changes; that Pvalb+ neurons subtractively suppress sensory responses, while Sst+ neurons divisively suppress sensory responses; that both populations of interneurons produce divisive changes; or that a single population of interneurons can produce both divisive and subtractive changes

span.label: qualifies → in vitro demonstrations that somatic and dendritic inhibition suppress single pyramidal neurons divisively and subtractively
span.quote: This may explain how we can observe such similar distributions of linear suppression types in vivo, even though activating Pvalb+ or Sst+ interneurons produces easily distinguishable forms of suppression in vitro.

span.label: contradicts → the standard prediction that activating Pvalb and Sst interneurons implements divisive and subtractive suppression respectively
span.quote: Based on the relationship between suppression type, synapse location, and the morphology of Pvalb+ and Sst+ interneurons, the standard prediction would be that activating Pvalb+ and Sst+ interneurons should implement divisive and subtractive forms of suppression, respectively.

span.label: divisive —contrasted-with→ subtractive
span.quote: In a subtractively suppressed neuron, this best-fit line will have a slope of 1 and a y-intercept significantly less than 0, while in a divisively suppressed neuron, the best-fit line will have a slope significantly less than 1 and a y-intercept not significantly different from 0.

span.label: RETRACTED (NOT A CONTAINMENT RELATION) · Sst —part-of→ dendrites
span.quote: Sst is expressed in roughly 25% of cortical inhibitory interneurons, including interneuron subtypes that avoid synapsing onto excitatory neurons’ somata and instead form contacts on their (mainly distal) dendrites

span.label: RETRACTED (NOT A CONTAINMENT RELATION, same shape as [1]) · Pvalb —part-of→ soma
span.quote: In contrast, Pvalb is expressed in roughly ~50% of cortical inhibitory interneurons, including subtypes whose axons form “baskets,” enfolding the soma in a dense net of inhibitory synapses, or “chandeliers,” enfolding the axon initial segment

span.label: soma —causes→ input resistance
span.quote: Because action potentials are generated near the soma, activating inhibitory conductances near the soma decreases the effective input resistance and thus divisively scales the magnitude of depolarization evoked by a particular synaptic conductance. This means that proportionately larger input currents are necessary to reach threshold ( Vu and Krasne, 1992 ; Jadi et al., 2012 ) and yields an overall divisive suppression of firing rates.

span.label: dendrites —distinct-from→ input resistance
span.quote: Because dendrites are electrotonically distant from the site of action potential generation, activating inhibitory conductances only in the dendrites will not substantially decrease the effective input resistance for more proximally delivered excitation. Because dendritic inhibition does not decrease somatic resistance, dendritic inhibition would be predicted to subtractively suppress the firing rate

span.label: RETRACTED (THE PAPER REPORTS THAT THE PREDICTED CONTRAST IS ABSENT, AND THE EDGE ASSERTS THE CONTRAST) · Sst —contrasted-with→ Pvalb
span.quote: The proportions of suppression types observed (divisive, subtractive, both, or neither) when activating Sst+ interneurons were not significantly different from that observed when activating Pvalb+ interneurons (g-test p = 0.54).

span.label: interneuron —part-of→ network
span.quote: Here, we demonstrate the critical, and occasionally counterintuitive, role of network interactions in determining the systems-level effects of neuron-level manipulations. We have demonstrated that non-linear networks readily obscure linear suppression type and that inhibition of neurons’ excitatory inputs provides a parsimonious explanation for the complex and apparently contradictory consequences of activating Sst+ or Pvalb+ interneurons in auditory cortex.

span.label: threshold —causes→ divisive
span.quote: As one example of such a mechanism, we used a simple network model to show that threshold nonlinearities can interact with inhibition to transform subtractive inhibition of neurons into divisive inhibition of networks, or vice versa. Varying just two properties of the model neuron (its threshold and the overall strength of suppression of its inputs) could cause the apparent linear effect of inhibition to be divisive, subtractive, or both

span.label: network —causes→ suppression
span.quote: The character of suppression in higher-order neurons was determined by their intrinsic properties and connections, regardless of whether the suppression in first-order neurons was divisive or subtractive— in other words, the characteristics of response inhibition specific to a single interneuron type can be “masked” by the network configuration and cellular properties of the network in which they are embedded.

span.label: in vitro —distinct-from→ suppression
span.quote: This may explain how we can observe such similar distributions of linear suppression types in vivo, even though activating Pvalb+ or Sst+ interneurons produces easily distinguishable forms of suppression in vitro.

span.label: Sst —causes→ bandwidth
span.quote: Across the populations, activating either Sst+ or Pvalb+ interneurons significantly narrowed bandwidths (median ± MAD: Ai32/Sst: control: 2.8 ± 0.7 octaves, activation: 2.3 ± 0.7 octaves, sign-rank p < 0.001; Ai32/Pvalb: control: 2.8 ± 0.6 octaves, activation 2.0 ± 0.7 octaves, sign-rank p < 0.001; Figures 3D and 3H ). The distribution of bandwidth changes when activating Sst+ interneurons was not significantly different from that observed when activating Pvalb+ interneurons

span.label: RETRACTED (`g-test --operationalised-as--> suppression`) · g-test —operationalised-as→ suppression
span.quote: The proportions of suppression types observed (divisive, subtractive, both, or neither) when activating Sst+ interneurons were not significantly different from that observed when activating Pvalb+ interneurons (g-test p = 0.54).

span.label: RETRACTED (THE SPAN ASSERTS SIMILARITY, THE EDGE ASSERTS CONTRAST) · anesthetized —contrasted-with→ awake
span.quote: The similarity of the data in the anesthetized and the awake preparation, despite the fact that some of the optogenetic parameters (light strength, optical fiber diameter) were not identical between the two conditions, suggests that this masking may be relatively robust.

span.label: ChR2 —operationalised-as→ Sst
span.quote: In order to compare the effects of Pvalb+ versus Sst+ neuron activation in an interconnected network, we produced mice in which Sst+ or Pvalb+ interneurons could be optogenetically activated by crossing strains that express Cre-recombinase under control of Sst or Pvalb promoters ( Taniguchi et al., 2011 ) with a strain in which expression of ChR2-eYFP is Cre dependent (Ai32)

span.label: A1 —part-of→ auditory cortex
span.quote: Primary auditory cortex (A1) was identified by using multiunit recordings of responses to tones of different frequencies and intensities to identify the short-latency (<12 ms) tonotopically organized auditory region caudal to the main frequency reversal.

span.label: tuning curves —operationalised-as→ inhibition
span.quote: In a threshold-linear response framework, when neurons’ responses are described in terms of canonical “tuning curves” relating their synaptic or sensory inputs to their spiking outputs, other factors such as synaptic inhibition are then characterized in terms of their effects on the scale or offset of these curves

span.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
span.quote: Unless otherwise noted, tests of whether light significantly affected a population of units were sign-rank tests; tests of whether continuous parameters were differently distributed between groups were rank-sum tests; tests of whether similar proportions of units were significantly affected by light were performed using Fisher’s exact test, except when testing for significant differences in the distributions of linear suppression types (proportional, absolute, both, neither), for which a g-test was used.

span.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
span.quote: The distribution of bandwidth changes when activating Sst+ interneurons was not significantly different from that observed when activating Pvalb+ interneurons (rank-sum p = 0.63, Figure 3I ).

span.label: G-test of independence
span.quote: The proportions of suppression types observed (divisive, subtractive, both, or neither) when activating Sst+ interneurons were not significantly different from that observed when activating Pvalb+ interneurons (g-test p = 0.54).

span.label: bootstrap
span.quote: For all other metrics, we performed bootstrap analysis to determine whether the changes observed in individual units were significant: we repeatedly (500 times) randomly reassigned trials to the light-off and light-on conditions and recalculated the response metric for each reassignment.

span.label: regression
span.quote: (Major axis regression was necessary to account for the measurement variance on both the x and y axis, which ordinary least-squares regression does not [ Sokal and Rohlf, 2012 ].)

span.label: t-test
span.quote: Significance of regression parameters was determined based on a t test of the parameter distribution as in Sokal and Rohlf (2012) with α = 0.05.

span.label: coefficient of determination
span.quote: Cumulative distribution of r 2 values (i.e., quality of linear fit) in Ai32/Sst (blue) and Ai32/Pvalb (red) mice shows that a linear fit accounts for a high proportion of the total variance of suppression.

span.label: permutation test
span.quote: as determined by a permutation test between control and light-activation trials, α = 0.05.

span.label: Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons
span.quote: The firing rate in each time bin was compared against the time bins in the 100 ms preceding the tone by a ranksum test with α = 0.001 (after Bonferroni-adjusted multiple comparisons corrections).

span.label: confidence interval
span.quote: The data in the regression plots are represented as lines of best-fit with 95% confidence intervals.

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: Data are represented as mean ± SEM.

span.label: g-test
span.quote: The proportions of suppression types observed (divisive, subtractive, both, or neither) when activating Sst+ interneurons were not significantly different from that observed when activating Pvalb+ interneurons (g-test p = 0.54).

span.label: rank-sum
span.quote: Across the populations, activating either Sst+ or Pvalb+ interneurons significantly narrowed bandwidths (median ± MAD: Ai32/Sst: control: 2.8 ± 0.7 octaves, activation: 2.3 ± 0.7 octaves, sign-rank p < 0.001; Ai32/Pvalb: control: 2.8 ± 0.6 octaves, activation 2.0 ± 0.7 octaves, sign-rank p < 0.001; Figures 3D and 3H ). The distribution of bandwidth changes when activating Sst+ interneurons was not significantly different from that observed when activating Pvalb+ interneurons

span.label: sign-rank
span.quote: Across the populations, activating either Sst+ or Pvalb+ interneurons significantly narrowed bandwidths (median ± MAD: Ai32/Sst: control: 2.8 ± 0.7 octaves, activation: 2.3 ± 0.7 octaves, sign-rank p < 0.001; Ai32/Pvalb: control: 2.8 ± 0.6 octaves, activation 2.0 ± 0.7 octaves, sign-rank p < 0.001; Figures 3D and 3H ). The distribution of bandwidth changes when activating Sst+ interneurons was not significantly different from that observed when activating Pvalb+ interneurons

span.label: Optogenetically activating either somatostatin- or parvalbumin-positive interneurons produced a mixture of divisive and subtractive suppression of auditory cortical tone responses, and neurons recorded at the same time were often suppressed in qualitatively different ways.
span.quote: In both awake and anesthetized animals, we found that activating either family of interneurons produced mixtures of divisive and subtractive effects and that simultaneously recorded neurons were often suppressed in qualitatively different ways.

span.label: The proportions of divisive, subtractive, mixed and neither-type suppression were statistically indistinguishable between Sst+ and Pvalb+ activation, contradicting the standard prediction that Pvalb+ cells divide and Sst+ cells subtract.
span.quote: The proportions of suppression types observed (divisive, subtractive, both, or neither) when activating Sst+ interneurons were not significantly different from that observed when activating Pvalb+ interneurons (g-test p = 0.54).

span.label: About half of suppressed units showed divisive-only suppression (slope below 1 with intercept not below 0), with the remainder split between subtractive-only, mixed, and neither, for both interneuron families.
span.quote: Approximately half of units showed only divisive but not subtractive suppression (slope < 1, intercept not significantly less than 0 in Ai32/Sst: n = 35 of 76 units; Ai32/Pvalb: n = 27 of 63 units; Figures 2E and 2H ).

span.label: A threshold-linear (slope-plus-intercept) description captured most of the variance of suppression for both interneuron types, so the suppression of individual neurons was well described as a linear transformation.
span.quote: We observed that these linear components accounted for a high proportion of the total variance of suppression in both Ai32/Pvalb and Ai32/Sst mouse strains ( Figure 2C ), implying that suppression of individual neurons evoked by either Sst or Pvalb neurons can be described in a linear framework.

span.label: Activating either interneuron family narrowed the frequency tuning bandwidths of other units in anesthetized mice, and the bandwidth changes did not differ between the two families.
span.quote: The distribution of bandwidth changes when activating Sst+ interneurons was not significantly different from that observed when activating Pvalb+ interneurons (rank-sum p = 0.63, Figure 3I ).

span.label: Slope, intercept and bandwidth changes were uncorrelated across pairs of neurons recorded simultaneously on the same probe, showing that neurons in one cortical column are not affected uniformly by the same interneuron activation.
span.quote: This shows that neurons within a cortical column are not equally affected by broad interneuron activation and that the resulting changes in the network are not uniform across columns.

span.label: In the network model, divisive suppression of inputs and subtractive suppression of inputs both produce divisive-like suppression of the net drive reaching a downstream neuron, because rectification makes subtractive suppression bite hardest at each input's preferred frequency.
span.quote: This implies that both divisive and subtractive mechanisms operating at the level of single cells can produce divisive-like suppression of the net drive to a neuron embedded in the network.

span.label: In the model, the observed suppression type of a downstream neuron was set by its own spiking threshold and the overall strength of suppression of its inputs rather than by whether its inputs were suppressed divisively or subtractively, so an interneuron type's signature is masked by network and cellular properties.
span.quote: The character of suppression in higher-order neurons was determined by their intrinsic properties and connections, regardless of whether the suppression in first-order neurons was divisive or subtractive— in other words, the characteristics of response inhibition specific to a single interneuron type can be “masked” by the network configuration and cellular properties of the network in which they are embedded.

span.label: activating either interneuron class produced mixtures of divisive and subtractive suppression rather than one or the other
span.quote: However, in both strains, we observed a mixture of divisive, sub-tractive, and mixed suppression. Approximately half of units showed only divisive but not subtractive suppression (slope < 1, intercept not significantly less than 0 in Ai32/Sst: n = 35 of 76 units; Ai32/Pvalb: n = 27 of 63 units; Figures 2E and 2H ). Of the remainder, some showed only subtractive but not divisive suppression (slope not significantly less than 1, intercept significantly less than 0 in Ai32/Sst: n = 12 of 76 units; Ai32/ Pvalb: n = 11 of 63 units; Figure 2F and 2I ); some showed both divisive and subtractive suppression (slope significantly less than 1, intercept significantly less than 0 in Ai32/Sst: n = 13 of 76 units; Ai32/Pvalb: n = 16 of 63 units; Figure 2G ); and in some units, neither subtractive nor divisive components were significant

span.label: the proportions of suppression types did not differ between the two classes, g-test p = 0.54
span.quote: The proportions of suppression types observed (divisive, subtractive, both, or neither) when activating Sst+ interneurons were not significantly different from that observed when activating Pvalb+ interneurons (g-test p = 0.54).

span.label: a linear framework accounted for a high proportion of the variance of suppression in both strains
span.quote: We observed that these linear components accounted for a high proportion of the total variance of suppression in both Ai32/Pvalb and Ai32/Sst mouse strains ( Figure 2C ), implying that suppression of individual neurons evoked by either Sst or Pvalb neurons can be described in a linear framework.

span.label: both classes narrowed frequency tuning bandwidths, and the distributions of change did not differ
span.quote: Across the populations, activating either Sst+ or Pvalb+ interneurons significantly narrowed bandwidths (median ± MAD: Ai32/Sst: control: 2.8 ± 0.7 octaves, activation: 2.3 ± 0.7 octaves, sign-rank p < 0.001; Ai32/Pvalb: control: 2.8 ± 0.6 octaves, activation 2.0 ± 0.7 octaves, sign-rank p < 0.001; Figures 3D and 3H ). The distribution of bandwidth changes when activating Sst+ interneurons was not significantly different from that observed when activating Pvalb+ interneurons

span.label: THE DECISIVE OBSERVATION: neurons recorded simultaneously on one probe were suppressed in uncorrelated ways
span.quote: Furthermore, we observed that even within a single recording, activation of Sst+ or Pvalb+ interneurons could produce diverse effects. For each pair of simultaneously recorded light-suppressed neurons ( Figure 4 ), we compared the effect of interneuron activation on the change in slope of the input-output relationship (i.e., the strength of multiplicative suppression), the change in y-inter-cept (i.e., the strength of subtractive suppression), and the change in FTP bandwidth ( Figure 4C ). None of these parameters were substantially correlated ( Figure 4A , slope: Ai32/Sst: n = 77, r 2 < 0.01, p = 0.67; Ai32/Pvalb: n = 56, r 2 < 0.01, p = 0.94; Figure 4B , y-intercept coefficients: Ai32/Sst: n = 77, r 2 = 0.06, p = 0.04; Ai32/Pvalb: n = 56, r 2 < 0.01, p = 0.67; Figure 4C , bandwidth: Ai32/Sst: n = 78, r 2 = 0.13, p = 0.001; Ai32/Pvalb: n = 53, r 2 < 0.01, p = 0.88). This shows that neurons within a cortical column are not equally affected by broad interneuron activation and that the resulting changes in the network are not uniform across columns.

span.label: which rules out preparation and animal-to-animal variability, and the same was seen in awake animals
span.quote: This variability is unlikely to be an artifact of animal-to-animal variability in the experimental preparation, because the characteristics of suppression in simultaneously recorded cells were not strongly correlated ( Figure 4 ), and it is unlikely to be associated only with a specific anesthetic condition because we observed it in awake animals as well.

span.label: THE PREDICTION THAT FAILED: anatomy predicts Pvalb divisive and Sst subtractive, and this is confirmed in vitro on single cells
span.quote: Based on the relationship between suppression type, synapse location, and the morphology of Pvalb+ and Sst+ interneurons, the standard prediction would be that activating Pvalb+ and Sst+ interneurons should implement divisive and subtractive forms of suppression, respectively.

span.label: the proposed explanation is that most cortical input is intracortical, so inhibition changes a neuron's inputs as well as the neuron
span.quote: To explain this observation, we note that cortical neurons are densely interconnected: the majority of cortical neurons receive the majority of their inputs from intracortical or feedback connections rather than from feedforward thalamocortical projections ( Benshalom and White, 1986 ; Abeles, 1991 ). Thus, although changes in inhibitory tone may have the predicted linear effect on neurons’ responses to any particular current or conductance, they also change the firing properties of the majority of these neurons’ converging/recurrent inputs and may thus have effects on responses qualitatively different from those predicted by single-neuron models.

span.label: and a network model shows that varying only threshold and input suppression strength moves the apparent effect between divisive and subtractive
span.quote: As one example of such a mechanism, we used a simple network model to show that threshold nonlinearities can interact with inhibition to transform subtractive inhibition of neurons into divisive inhibition of networks, or vice versa. Varying just two properties of the model neuron (its threshold and the overall strength of suppression of its inputs) could cause the apparent linear effect of inhibition to be divisive, subtractive, or both

span.label: so a class's characteristic suppression can be MASKED by the network it sits in
span.quote: The character of suppression in higher-order neurons was determined by their intrinsic properties and connections, regardless of whether the suppression in first-order neurons was divisive or subtractive— in other words, the characteristics of response inhibition specific to a single interneuron type can be “masked” by the network configuration and cellular properties of the network in which they are embedded.

span.label: this reconciles the in vitro clarity with the in vivo mixture rather than treating the discrepancy as a problem
span.quote: This may explain how we can observe such similar distributions of linear suppression types in vivo, even though activating Pvalb+ or Sst+ interneurons produces easily distinguishable forms of suppression in vitro.

span.label: the visual cortex literature contains every combination of the two assignments, described as apparently irreconcilable
span.quote: Studies in primary visual cortex (V1) have produced diverse and even apparently irreconcilable findings regarding the effects of activating Sst+ and Pvalb+ interneurons on single unit responses. Various studies have shown that Pvalb+ neurons’ activation may change other neurons’ sensory responses divisively, while Sst+ neurons’ activation produces subtractive changes; that Pvalb+ neurons subtractively suppress sensory responses, while Sst+ neurons divisively suppress sensory responses; that both populations of interneurons produce divisive changes; or that a single population of interneurons can produce both divisive and subtractive changes

span.label: the same masking should appear in any network of appreciable complexity, and several further routes to it are named
span.quote: Note that this second-order effect of inhibitory activity on excitatory tuning is merely one among many mechanisms by which this “masking” phenomenon may emerge. Additional sources of obfuscation are abundant in the cortical literature. For example, many types of interneuron are themselves tuned and receive organized excitation from local cortical networks ( Thomson et al., 2002 ; Holmgren et al., 2003 ; Yoshimura and Callaway, 2005 ; Stokes and Isaacson, 2010 ; Moore and Wehr, 2013 ; Lee et al., 2014 ); manipulations that change the tuning of cortical excitation will themselves change the tuning of cortical interneurons, producing third- and higher-order effects. In addition, many types of cortical interneurons selectively inhibit one another; activation of one type may thus reduce the inhibition originating from others, producing complex changes in activity and tuning ( Jiang et al., 2013 ; Lee et al., 2013 ; Pi et al., 2013 ; Xu et al., 2013 ; Fu et al., 2014 ). It is thus likely that similar masking phenomena will be observed in any network of appreciable complexity.

span.label: local subnetworks can interpret the same inhibition differently even inside one global network
span.quote: This indicates that even in the same global network, local subnetworks of neurons with different intrinsic or connectional properties can selectively and differentially interpret the inhibition provided by a given population of interneurons.

span.label: anaesthetised and awake preparations agreed despite differing optogenetic parameters, suggesting the masking is robust
span.quote: The similarity of the data in the anesthetized and the awake preparation, despite the fact that some of the optogenetic parameters (light strength, optical fiber diameter) were not identical between the two conditions, suggests that this masking may be relatively robust.

span.label: SCOPE STATED: both populations were driven nonselectively and diffusely in time, so natural differences in their dynamics could not show up
span.quote: However, we note that in this experiment both populations of interneurons were activated in a nonselective and temporally diffuse manner; it is likely that during normal brain operation, functional differences between interneuron types will emerge from differences in their response properties and temporal dynamics.
